description.summary: A Japanese yōkai of a woman who died in or shortly after childbirth, who appears at night carrying a baby and tries to pass it to a passerby; the bundle then turns to leaves, stones, or grows unbearably heavy.
description.full: Ubume (産女, 'birthing woman') is a yōkai of Japanese folklore, classified among the yūrei (ghosts) of women who died during pregnancy or in childbirth. She appears most often at night, beside roads, bridges, or rivers, in the form of a pale, blood-stained woman wearing a red waist cloth and cradling an infant. She approaches travelers and asks them to hold her baby; once the bundle is taken it grows progressively heavier, or transforms on examination into a bundle of leaves, a stone, or a buddha-statue. In other accounts she buys candy at a shop with leaf-money for a child whom locals later find buried with a real living infant in his mother's grave. The Ubume is rarely portrayed as purely malevolent — she is moved by maternal grief and the unfulfilled obligation to her child — and compassion shown to her can lay her spirit to rest. The earliest written account is in the 12th-century Konjaku Monogatarishū, where the warrior Urabe no Suetake encounters an ubume crossing a river. The yōkai's iconography is also strongly shaped by the Chinese-derived bird-spirit Kokakuchō (姑獲鳥), introduced to Japan via texts such as the Wakan Sansai Zue (1712).

etymology.origin: The name 'ubume' is written 産女 ('birthing woman'). It is also written with the Chinese-derived 姑獲鳥 ('kokakuchō'), originally a Chinese bird-spirit absorbed into the Japanese ubume tradition during the medieval period.
etymology.meaning: 'Birthing woman'; the alternative writing 姑獲鳥 carries the sense of a bird-form spirit that snatches children
etymology.first_use: Earliest extant Japanese attestation: Konjaku Monogatarishū (early 12th century)

related_phenomena.name: Kokakuchō (姑獲鳥)
related_phenomena.description: Chinese-derived bird-form spirit that snatches children; merged with the ubume tradition in Edo-period Japan

related_phenomena.name: Pontianak
related_phenomena.description: Southeast Asian (Malay/Indonesian) ghost of a woman who died in childbirth

related_phenomena.name: La Llorona
related_phenomena.description: Latin American weeping mother spirit, sharing themes of maternal death and lost children

related_phenomena.name: Yūrei (general)
related_phenomena.description: Broader category of Japanese ghosts to which ubume belongs

features.description: Often depicted naked from the waist up or wearing a blood-soaked red waist cloth, marking the manner of her death
Carries a baby — sometimes a real living infant, sometimes an illusory bundle that becomes leaves or stones
Through Chinese influence, occasionally depicted with bird-like features or wings; described as a gull-like creature appearing on rainy nights with eerie flames
On Iki, ubume appear as a swaying blue light rather than as a clearly humanoid figure

physical.morphology: Anthropomorphic woman of normal size, frequently with disheveled hair and bloodied lower body; some regional and Chinese-derived variants are bird-like or appear as glowing apparitions.

abilities.description: Hands a bundle (her 'baby') to a passerby; the bundle either grows progressively heavier or transforms into leaves, stones, or a stone buddha
In the candy-buying variant, pays for sweets with money that later turns to leaves
Manifests near rivers, crossroads, or the site where she died, especially at night
Compassionate response (taking and caring for the child, performing Buddhist rites) can lay her spirit to rest

habitat_preference: the site of the woman's death
candy and sweet shops (in the candy-variant tales)
behavior.diet: Folkloric: not depicted as feeding; her actions are driven by maternal grief and obligation rather than hunger.
patterns: Approaches lone travelers at night and asks them to hold her child
Visits a shop nightly to buy candy with leaf-money
Returns to the place of her death until rites are performed for her and her child
Resolved by compassion, Buddhist memorial services, or proper burial of mother and infant together

range.description: Found across Japan with regional variants and overlaps with Chinese-derived bird-spirit traditions.

hotspots.name: Iki Island

location.description: Island in the Tsushima Strait, Nagasaki Prefecture

hotspots.notes: Local variant 'unme' / 'uume' — appears as a swaying blue light when a young person or pregnant woman dies in difficult childbirth.

peak_activity_periods.description: Ubume becomes a stock figure of yōkai painting and ghost-story collections; absorbs Chinese kokakuchō imagery
Reframed in horror literature, manga, anime, and film (notably Natsuhiko Kyōgoku's Ubume no Natsu, 1994)

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Often associated with summer ghost-story traditions (kaidan).

origins.cultural_roots: Ubume sit at the intersection of Japanese fears of maternal mortality, Buddhist concern for the salvation of mothers and infants who died in childbirth, and Chinese bird-spirit lore (kokakuchō) absorbed during the medieval and Edo periods.
origins.earliest_accounts: The earliest extant tale is in the early-12th-century Konjaku Monogatarishū, in which the warrior Urabe no Suetake meets an ubume at a river crossing while on military duty.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to broader yūrei tradition; absorbed Chinese kokakuchō through encyclopedic works such as the Wakan Sansai Zue (1712); paralleled by the Southeast Asian pontianak / kuntilanak.

timeline.event: Earliest extant ubume tale recorded in Konjaku Monogatarishū (Urabe no Suetake encounters the ubume at a river)
Terajima Ryōan publishes Wakan Sansai Zue, identifying the ubume with the Chinese kokakuchō and giving it a bird-spirit description
timeline.significance: Major synthesis of Chinese and Japanese strands

timeline.event: Toriyama Sekien depicts the ubume in his Edo-period yōkai compendium Gazu Hyakki Yagyō
Natsuhiko Kyōgoku publishes the novel Ubume no Natsu (The Summer of the Ubume), launching his Kyōgokudō series
timeline.significance: Major contemporary literary reframing of the figure

history.modern_era: The ubume remains a recurring figure in Japanese horror literature, film, and games, often invoked to explore themes of maternal grief, social anxiety around pregnancy and miscarriage, and Buddhist cosmology of unsaved infants (mizuko).

notable.name: Urabe no Suetake meets the ubume

location.description: A river crossing in central Japan

credibility_factors: Recorded in canonical Heian tale collection

notable.description: While crossing a river at night on military duty, the warrior Urabe no Suetake encounters a woman who asks him to hold her baby. He accepts and holds the bundle calmly; the apparition cannot frighten him and disappears.

factors: Canonical folklore narrative, not a verifiable encounter
credibility.notes: Earliest extant ubume tale and a touchstone of the tradition.

documentary.name: Konjaku Monogatarishū account
documentary.analysis: Verified as an early-12th-century textual record of the tradition; not evidence of an objective encounter.

documentary.name: Wakan Sansai Zue (1712) entry on the ubume / kokakuchō
documentary.description: Edo-period encyclopedic treatment that fuses the ubume with the Chinese kokakuchō.
documentary.analysis: Key text in the canonization of Edo-era ubume iconography.

paranormal.name: Onryō / unsettled spirit
paranormal.description: Within Japanese folk Buddhism, ubume are real spirits of women whose violent or unsatisfied deaths bind them to the world until proper rites (especially mizuko kuyō for the lost infant) release them.
evidence_cited: Ritual practices for unborn and infant dead

skeptical.name: Cultural processing of maternal mortality
skeptical.description: Ubume folklore encodes pre-modern Japan's high maternal and infant mortality rates and the cultural anxiety around women dying in childbirth.
evidence_cited: Concentration of ubume tales near rivers and bridges, where pregnant women's bodies were sometimes buried separately

skeptical.name: Hybrid with Chinese bird-spirit
skeptical.description: Many of the more elaborate ubume features (bird-form, eerie flames, gull-like behavior) are imported from the Chinese kokakuchō tradition rather than indigenous Japanese folklore.
evidence_cited: Wakan Sansai Zue's explicit identification of ubume with the kokakuchō

traditions: Edo-period yōkai painting and woodblock culture
Folk Buddhist mizuko kuyō (memorial rites for unborn or dead infants)
stories: Urabe no Suetake's encounter at the river (Konjaku Monogatarishū)
The candy-buying ghost (kosodate yūrei): a dead mother buys candy nightly for her infant buried alive in her grave
Toriyama Sekien's depiction of the ubume in Gazu Hyakki Yagyō
folklore.beliefs: Pregnant women who died in or before childbirth required special rites — including, traditionally, the removal and burial of the fetus with the mother — to prevent the spirit from becoming an ubume.

indigenous.significance: Ubume traditions express Japanese cosmological concern for the mother–child bond, salvation of the dead, and the dangers of liminal spaces (rivers, bridges, crossroads).
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Modern English-language treatments sometimes reduce the ubume to a horror trope; the figure has long been understood as tragic and worthy of compassion within Japanese tradition.

literature: Lafcadio Hearn (1899) — In Ghostly Japan (related kosodate-yūrei tales)
Natsuhiko Kyōgoku (1994) — Ubume no Natsu (The Summer of the Ubume)
film_tv: Ubume no Natsu / The Summer of the Ubume (2005, dir. Akio Jissoji)
Numerous appearances in Japanese horror anthology series and yōkai documentaries
games: Various Japanese yōkai-themed video games and tabletop games
other: Mizuko kuyō rituals at Buddhist temples for unborn and infant dead, sometimes invoking ubume imagery
